name: Grape seed extract

lead: Grape seed extract is a supplement made from grape seeds, rich in procyanidin polyphenols. People take it as an antioxidant for healthier, younger-looking skin, and some forum users add it hoping to lower estrogen via aromatase inhibition.

Procyanidins scavenge free radicals in lab tests, and cell studies show inhibition of aromatase and digestive enzymes. Human trials are small and have looked at blood pressure, lipids, vascular stiffness and exercise rather than appearance. Effects on estrogen in humans have not been published.

paras: It is taken as daily capsules, and it also appears as an ingredient in topical skin products. Users add it to skin or antioxidant routines and generally give it weeks to months.
Reported effects are mild, such as stomach upset and headache, according to secondary sources, with possible interactions with anticoagulants. It is sold as a dietary supplement in the US.

angle.text: Grape seed extract is taken as a polyphenol antioxidant: less oxidative damage is meant to leave skin healthier and younger-looking, and some forum users also use it as an aromatase inhibitor to lower estrogen. The case comes from lab data.

lead: Grape seed extract (GSE) is a dietary supplement made from the seeds of grapes, mainly Vitis vinifera, which are a by-product of winemaking and grape-juice production. Its polyphenol fraction, typically 5-8% of the seed by weight, consists largely of flavan-3-ols such as catechin and epicatechin and their oligomers and polymers, known as procyanidins or oligomeric proanthocyanidin complexes. [1][2]

It is sold as oral capsules and as an ingredient in topical products, and is marketed for antioxidant, vascular and skin-related purposes. In looksmaxxing forums it appears mainly in discussions of skin health and of aromatase inhibition, a claim drawn from laboratory studies. [3][4]

Published human trials of GSE are generally small and have examined outcomes such as blood pressure, lipids, vascular stiffness and exercise performance; no published trial found in the sources reviewed tests it for appearance outcomes such as wrinkles or skin tone. Much of the biological work on it comes from cell and animal studies. [5][3]
infobox: Dietary supplement; also an ingredient in some OTC homeopathic-style products

paras: Grape seeds contain lipids, protein, carbohydrate and roughly 5-8% polyphenols depending on variety. The polyphenols are mainly gallic acid, monomeric flavan-3-ols (catechin, epicatechin, gallocatechin, epigallocatechin and epicatechin gallate) and procyanidin dimers, trimers and larger polymers. [2] Commercial extracts are generally standardised to a procyanidin percentage. Procyanidin C1, a trimer present in small amounts, has been studied separately in cell and mouse experiments. [6]

GSE is marketed as an antioxidant and for vascular health. Some topical and oral products pair it with other ingredients; one US-listed bruise-support product combines GSE with arnica, bromelain, vitamin C, rutin and zinc oxide and states that it reduces pain, swelling and discolouration from bruises. [7] The label evidence for that combination is the manufacturer's statement, not a published trial of GSE alone.

In laboratory work, grape seed polyphenols scavenge free radicals and inhibit lipid peroxidation. [2][2] Extracts have also inhibited the digestive enzymes alpha-amylase and alpha-glucosidase in vitro. [8] Procyanidin oligomers have been absorbed and metabolised in animal studies, and absorption of procyanidin dimers and trimers has been examined in rats and in food-matrix models. [9][10] A laboratory study reported that GSE inhibited aromatase activity and reduced aromatase mRNA levels in breast cancer cell lines and reduced tumour growth in a mouse xenograft model. [4]

A 2002 safety evaluation of a proanthocyanidin-rich grape seed extract in toxicology models is available. [5] Grokipedia, an AI-generated reference, reports mild gastrointestinal upset, headache or dizziness as the usual complaints and notes possible interactions with anticoagulants and cytochrome P450 substrates; this is unverified secondary information. [1]

Registered human studies of GSE have examined effects on estrogen levels in postmenopausal women, blood pressure in pre-hypertension, lipid profile and oxidised LDL in hyperlipidaemia, arterial stiffness in obese adults, muscle metaboreflex and cycling performance, and prostate-specific antigen in prostate cancer patients. [11][12][13][14][15] A dental trial has tested GSE as a collagen cross-linker before veneer bonding. [16] A 2022 systematic review of 19 randomised trials is reported to have found modest reductions in diastolic but not systolic blood pressure. [1] No studies found on appearance outcomes such as wrinkles, skin elasticity or facial aesthetics.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, GSE is mentioned mainly as a possible natural aromatase inhibitor, based on a laboratory paper shared in a forum thread. [4]

claims.claim: Grape seed extract works as an aromatase inhibitor and so can lower estrogen.
